title: Curbcut
pitch: Curbcut gives developers and ChatGPT a shared WebMCP workspace to inspect real axe findings, preview surgical fixes, preserve human judgment, and verify repairs together.
about_excerpt: Curbcut gives developers and ChatGPT a shared WebMCP workspace to inspect real axe findings, preview surgical fixes, preserve human judgment, and verify repairs together. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Scanned Workspace Mechanical Repair Preview Verified Mechanical Repair Blocked Agent Action Contextual Proposal Responsive Workspace Inspiration Accessibility scanners are good at finding problems, but finding them is only the beginning. A developer still has to find the correct source code, understand the evidence, choose the correct repair, preview its effect, and check the result. We built Curbcut around the question: What if the developer and an external browser agent could work together on the same live accessibility workspace? The agent could handle repetitive technical work, while the developer maintained authority over changes that require meaning, context, or design judgment. What it does Curbcut is a browser-native accessibility repair workbench for static HTML and CSS. The workspace keeps everything together: Editable source A securely isolated live preview Real axe-core accessibility findings Exact source mapping and rendered-element highlighting Proposed code diffs A rendered preview of each proposed repair Human approval for semantic changes Fresh verification scans Exact Undo and clean source export A shared timeline of human and agent actions axe-core scans the actual rendered preview, and the results aren't hard-coded. Selecting an issue focuses its exact source range and highlights the corresponding element in the preview. Every repair begins as a non-mutating proposal. Curbcut shows the exact source diff and proposed visual result before changing the working source. Technical repairs, such as removing a positive tabindex, can be applied and verified in the code directly. Contextual repairs, including form labels, image alternatives, button names, and document text, remain blocked until the developer reviews and approves the exact proposal. If the browser agent attempts to apply a contextual proposal early, Curbcut returns APPROVAL_REQUIRED, visibly records the blocked action, and leaves the source unchanged. Curbcut exposes ten focused WebMCP tools covering the real workflow: workspace inspection, scanning, listing and inspecting issues, previewing, applying, rejecting, undoing, summarizing, and exporting. These tools operate on the same React store and preview used by the visible interface. There is no arbitrary JavaScript tool, arbitrary DOM mutation, or whole-document AI rewrite. How we built it Curbcut is a browser-only React 19, TypeScript, and Vite application deployed as a static site on Vercel. It requires no account, backend, or database, and the developer’s source stays local to the browser. We use parse5 8.0.1 to parse canonical HTML with source locations and assign revision-bound internal node IDs. Mapping metadata is added only to generated preview markup, so it never contaminates the working or exported source. Repairs use validated raw-offset patches that preserve unrelated source text. Imported HTML is treated as untrusted. DOMPurify sanitizes it before it enters an iframe with sandbox="allow-scripts" and no same-origin permission. A nonce-based Content Security Policy blocks network requests, navigation, forms, embeds, and untrusted scripts. axe-core 4.13.0 runs inside that opaque preview realm. A validated postMessage bridge connects scanning and highlighting to the React workspace while checking the channel, request ID, message shape, and source revision. The top-level page registers exactly ten WebMCP tools through document.modelContext. Inputs are runtime-validated, imported source and accessibility snippets are marked as untrusted content, stale revisions are rejected, and read-only tools use the appropriate annotations. Most importantly, the agent cannot manufacture human approval. Contextual approval tokens are created only when the developer approves the exact visible proposal through the interface. Challenges we ran into The first major challenge was executing axe inside an opaque sandbox while safely returning useful results to the parent application. We needed enough communication for rendering, scanning, and highlighting without granting the preview same-origin access. The second was reliable source mapping. Existing HTML IDs were not sufficient because imported documents can have missing or duplicate IDs. We instead built parser-backed mappings using exact source ranges and preview-only internal metadata. The third was keeping proposals bound to the correct source revision. Rendering, scanning, agent calls, and human actions are asynchronous, so Curbcut rejects stale issue and proposal IDs and requires the exact proposed preview to report ready before Apply becomes valid. Finally, we had to make the human-agent boundary technically enforceable. A prompt asking the agent to wait was not enough. The application itself had to reject unauthorized contextual changes and preserve the proposal and source unchanged. Accomplishments that we're proud of A real end-to-end WebMCP workflow where external browser-agent actions visibly update the same workspace the developer is reviewing Real axe scans against an isolated live preview rather than stored or fixture-specific results Exact mapping from rendered axe nodes to editable source without relying on user-provided IDs Small deterministic patches instead of whole-document model rewrites A visible, enforceable human-approval boundary for semantic changes Fresh rescan verification, exact Undo, and clean export Five bounded repair families, with color contrast intentionally kept as evidence rather than guessed automatically An unrelated imported profile-form test proving that the scanner and mapping system are not hard-coded to the checkout demo 88 passing unit and integration tests and 30 passing browser tests A 72-trajectory WebMCP evaluation with 69 operationally correct workflows, zero approval-boundary violations, and zero infrastructure failures A production deployment exercised through browser-agent tooling with all ten tools discoverable and no WebMCP console errors Curbcut does not claim automated WCAG compliance. A cleared automated finding proves only that the targeted automated check disappeared after a fresh scan. Manual review, assistive-technology testing, and disabled-user expertise remain essential. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes meaningful product actions rather than generic browser control. The browser agent does not replace the application; it gains a structured way to participate in the application’s existing workflow. We also learned that accessibility repair is as much an authority problem as a code-generation problem. Some changes are mechanical. video_transcript_excerpt: Scanners are great at finding accessibility problems, and agents are great at changing code, but someone still has to decide what a change should mean. Kurb Cut brings both into one shared workspace, where ChatGPT can inspect a real issue and preview a precise fix. Here we have 10 tools available for ChatGPT to call for WebMCP. Here, Axe finds the issues, Kurb Cut safely renders the page in the middle panel, maps it back to the exact source code on the left, and manages the repair. WebMCP is what lets ChatGPT use those same visible actions without any arbitrary code execution or any broad site-wide recites. Looking at the compact diff over here in the code, before anything changes, Kurb Cut shows us the proposed result and smallest possible diff. The working source is still untouched on the left, but since removing a positive tab index doesn't really invent any new content for meeting, this repair can be can proceed without any semantic approval. Now, ChatGPT applies that exact proposal and asks Kurb Cut to run Axe again. The source revision changes, and the tab index finding disappears. Notice the wording. Kurb Cut verifies this target automated check, but it never claims the whole page is WCAG compliant, since that requires real human testing and disability compliance. The missing email label is a more interesting case. Here, Kurb Cut finds visible near text that can turn it into a precise label association. So, we look over here at the label under the email address, we can see that Kurb Cut is trying to find text near it to get some relevant context for what label should be under here. Uh but, once it gives us suggestion, only a person can really confirm whether those words really describe the field correctly. ChatGPT can prepare the difference, like it said here, but it can't approve it for me. Now, it is requiring human approval on the bottom. To prove the boundary is real, I asked ChatGPT on the left to apply it anyways. But, as you will see, Kurb Cut will actually block the call. The source will actually stay untouched, and the proposal stays pending. That's an enforced product rule, not just a polite instruction in the system. md file. Now, I will approve the change myself. Now, I review the exact wording it used, source diff, and rendered preview, and I approve this one myself. So, now with the approval recorded, CurbCut can apply it, rescan, summarize, and change what it needs to be changed, and look at what needs to done. After that, it can export the clean HTML with none of CurbCut's internal mapping data, leaving your site clean. Looking at the remaining image alt, color contrast, button name, and HTML has lang problems. We can see that CurbCut knows when not to guess. Image purpose and contrast still need context, so those stay as review items, and the timeline at the bottom keeps the agent's actions and my approvals together, recorded. Finally, undo restores the exact previous source, not an approximate reverse edit. A fresh Axe scan brings the label finding back, proving that the evidence always reflects the current revision. CurbCut gives the agent the mechanical work and keeps meeting with the human, all inside the live browser workspace. Thank you.

live_observation.first_impression: Curbcut opens to an accessibility workspace with editable HTML source, a live preview, an evidence ledger listing six axe findings, and repair/export controls.
live_observation.action_attempted: Opened the CRITICAL button-name finding from the evidence ledger.
live_observation.after_state: The finding control responded while the workspace stayed on the same source/preview/ledger layout; no destructive repair was applied.
live_observation.notes: The demo visibly supports inspection of findings and includes separate controls for Rescan with axe, Undo last repair, Import files, export, and agent-prompt copying.
